content: 1. Monitoring and preventing toxicity associated with deoxycholate amphotericin B therapy is strongly recommended to minimize potential harm to patients. 2. For individuals with HIV experiencing mild to moderate histoplasmosis, itraconazole at a dose of 200 mg twice daily is recommended following a loading dose of 200 mg three times daily for three days. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty of evidence due to imprecision and indirectness. 3. According to the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines, this itraconazole regimen can also be applied to treat disseminated histoplasmosis in immunosuppressed individuals without HIV. 4. Maintenance therapy with itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for 12 months is recommended. However, shorter durations may be considered if the patient is clinically stable, on antiretroviral therapy (ART), has suppressed viral loads, and shows improved immune status. 5. Without maintenance therapy, relapse rates for disseminated histoplasmosis in people with HIV can reach up to 90%, often occurring 6–18 months after discontinuing induction therapy. 6. Antifungal maintenance therapy is essential to suppress residual infection and prevent relapse. Itraconazole has shown higher success rates (75%) compared to fluconazole (40%), although direct randomized comparisons are lacking. 7. A loading dose of itraconazole (200 mg three times daily for three days) is typically used to achieve steady-state concentrations more rapidly. 8. The optimal duration of maintenance therapy remains unclear and should be determined based on clinical judgment. Some national guidelines recommend lifelong antifungal therapy, especially in cases of poor adherence, low itraconazole levels, or central nervous system (CNS) involvement. 9. IDSA guidelines recommend azole-based maintenance therapy for one year. 10. A systematic review comparing 12 months of itraconazole maintenance therapy with shorter durations found limited evidence, with only one retrospective cohort study available. This study had a high risk of bias. 11. The recommendation for one year of itraconazole maintenance therapy is conditional, with very low certainty of evidence. The balance of effects was judged to favor the intervention, as it is both feasible and acceptable. 12. Itraconazole and dolutegravir, an antiretroviral drug, are not expected to have significant drug-drug interactions. 13. Shorter maintenance therapy courses (at least six months) may be considered for patients who are clinically stable, on ART, with suppressed viral loads and immune recovery (CD4 counts >200 cells/mm³). 14. Shortening maintenance therapy should be based on the patient’s response to ART, clinical resolution of histoplasmosis, and absence of significant drug-drug interactions. 15. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) associated with histoplasmosis is uncommon but can occur, typically within 60 days of initiating ART. Symptoms resemble disseminated histoplasmosis and include fever, weight loss, cough, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. 16. Management of histoplasmosis-associated IRIS includes continuing ART and ensuring optimal antifungal therapy. Short-course oral steroids (e.g., prednisone 1–2 mg/kg/day for 1–2 weeks) may be considered in life-threatening cases. 17. Coinfection with tuberculosis (TB) and histoplasmosis presents diagnostic and management challenges due to overlapping symptoms and potential drug-drug interactions, particularly between rifampicin and itraconazole. 18. Prompt treatment of TB and histoplasmosis coinfection is recommended, balancing the risks of Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistance and subtherapeutic itraconazole levels. 19. Monitoring itraconazole serum levels is advised to ensure adequate absorption, assess adherence, and evaluate the impact of drug-drug interactions. 20. Amphotericin B therapy requires careful monitoring for toxicity, including nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, infusion-related reactions, and anemia. Renal function should be evaluated regularly, and appropriate fluid and electrolyte management should be implemented. 21. Proactive management of amphotericin B toxicity, including extended infusion times and monitoring of renal function, has been associated with improved outcomes in patients. 22. Adverse effects of itraconazole include nausea, vomiting, rash, and pedal edema. Variable bioavailability is a limitation, and serum itraconazole levels should be monitored when possible. 23. Clinicians may consider alternative strategies, such as increasing itraconazole doses, extending amphotericin B induction therapy, or using other azole drugs (e.g., posaconazole, voriconazole, or fluconazole) in cases of drug-drug interactions or suboptimal itraconazole levels. 24. Replacing rifampicin with rifabutin may also be an option to mitigate drug-drug interactions. 25. Adjustments to treatment regimens may be necessary for patients experiencing toxicity, drug interactions, or resistance profiles requiring protease inhibitors or second-line anti-TB drugs. 26. Antiretroviral resistance genotyping and Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug susceptibility testing can assist in clinical decision-making when available. 27. Safe administration of amphotericin B formulations may require referral to specialized centers with resources to manage toxicity effectively.
